A subtle Swift Concurrency pitfall for developers using Point-Free's swift-dependencies. I recently tracked down a crash that only affected users running iOS 17. The stack trace pointed deep into Swift's concurrency runtime: swift_task_reportIllegalTaskLocalBindingWithinWithTaskGroup
None of my code interacted with task-local values directly. The only suspicious line was reading a @Dependency property from Point-Free's swift-dependencies library inside a withThrowingTaskGroup. The exact same code worked flawlessly on iOS 18. After digging into Swift's task-local behavior, the cause turned out to be surprisingly subtle. Reading a @Dependency property inside a withTaskGroup or withThrowingTaskGroup body including inside an addTask closure's capture list can crash on iOS 17 with a fatal swif…

entry.title: I built a macOS app on a 9 hour flight which renames your Downloads folder full of junk
entry.summary: I built a macOS app on a 9½ hour flight after work because I was tired of files named "Screenshot 2026-07-18 at 5.02.14 PM.png" My desktop had become a graveyard of "IMG_3461.png" and "Untitled document (17).txt." I knew none of them. Opening each one just to rename it was a chore I was never actually going to do. So I stopped renaming files by hand and built something that would. Waypost reads what's actually inside a file (text, scans, PDFs, images) and gives it a name that makes sense, sorts it into the right folder, and tags it. All using Apple Intelligence, running entirely on your Mac. No cloud, no upload. Your lease agreement, your tax docs, your half finished essay: none of it ever leaves your machine. Turn off WiFi and watch it keep working. Trust was the harder problem than renaming ever was. So I built in the controls I'd actually want: a toggle for every file type, naming conventions, folder-specific configuration, and an ask before renaming mode that suggests a name and waits for your click before touching anything. Swift for macOS. Next.js on Vercel for auth. Stripe for payments. $7, once, no subscription, because there's no server to keep paying for. Check it out: https://waypost.bymanu.me

entry.title: Sales Discovery for Founders: How to Talk to Users Before You Build
entry.summary:
You've built an app. A marketplace. A SaaS tool. But nobody's using it. Most Founders Skip This
So they: Ship a feature Wonder why nobody uses it Ship another feature Wonder why that doesn't work either Burn runway Die Meanwhile, founders who talk to users first do discovery before they code Phase 1: Before you build anything Talk to 20 potential users about their actual problem (not the problem you assumed) Ask: "What are you trying to solve? How are you solving it now? What gets in the way?" Phase 2: Present your idea Explain your solution to 5 of those users Ask: "Would you actually pay for this? When?" Phase 3: Build minimally Build the simplest version that solves their #1 problem Phase 4: Before scaling Have discovery conversations with 10 paying customers Confirm: Budget, Authority (are they the decider?), Needs (are we solving the right problem?), Timeline (are they sticking around?) Why This Matters for Founders Every feature you build is a bet. If you're betting blind, you're throwing money away. Founders who do discovery: Waste less engineering time Before you write one line of code, talk to 5 potential customers about their problem. Document their answers. Then build. Sounds slow. But it's way faster than building the wrong thing Check out this resource: https://www.amazon.com/Lean-Startup-Entrepreneurs-Continuous-Innovation/dp/0307887898

entry.summary: A prompt-cache write pays for itself after a single re-read within the TTL: the write bills 1.25x the input rate, the read bills 0.1x, so one hit already swings the two-call total from a 25% premium to a 32.5% saving.
